applied.old: The country appellation, used when the grapes come from more than one state; it may carry no vintage, and it is the bottom of the ladder and the origin of much bulk wine.
applied.new: The country appellation, used when the grapes come from more than one state; since a federal rule of November 2012 it may carry a vintage when 85 per cent of the wine is from that year, and it is the bottom of the ladder and the origin of much bulk wine.

The Village question c-il084y1r already teaches this, so the country article now follows it.

applied.old: Canadian icewine must be harvested at minus 8°C or colder, with the grapes frozen on the vine. Germany's Eiswein rule is minus 7°C, the figure most often swapped in.
applied.new: Canadian icewine must be harvested at minus 8°C or colder, with the grapes frozen on the vine. Minus 7°C, the figure most often swapped in, is the German Eiswein figure, given by its courts and wine institute; German law itself asks only that the grapes be frozen when picked and pressed.
applied.verification: verified by one search: the judgment of the Oberverwaltungsgericht Rheinland-Pfalz of 7 May 2014 (8 A 10489/13) holds that the law asks for grapes frozen at picking and pressing and reads minus 7°C over some ten to twelve hours as what the concentration of healthy grapes needs; no result shows a figure in the text of the Weingesetz or the Weinverordnung, and the German Wine Institute and the Bavarian state institute (LWG, Kurzleitfaden Eiswein, November 2025) give minus 7°C as the working figure. The wording therefore names the courts and the wine institute as the source of the figure and the law as asking only for frozen grapes, which stands whichever way the court reading is weighed. The direct integrator (applied-cms-direct.json) found secondary pages saying the law requires minus 7°C and left its upper bank recurrences; this search supports the finding.
applied.source: rechtslupe.de, Die erforderlichen Minusgrade bei Eiswein (OVG Rheinland-Pfalz, 7 May 2014, 8 A 10489/13); lwg.bayern.de, Kurzleitfaden Eiswein (20 November 2025); searched 31 October 2026

applied.old: Vino de Pago is a single estate's own appellation, not a tier above DOCa in prestige by law; it sits beside the DOs.
applied.new: Vino de Pago is a single estate's own appellation, which the 2003 law lists above DOCa: a level for one property, not a rung a region climbs to. A pago inside a DOCa may be called Vino de Pago Calificado.
applied.verification: verified by one search: the Ministry's review of the 2003 law (mapa.gob.es) lists the levels of the origin system in the order vinos de calidad con indicación geográfica, vinos con denominación de origen, vinos con denominación de origen calificada and vinos de pagos, vinos de pagos last and highest (vinos de la tierra below them all), the order of article 13 of Ley 24/2003 (BOE-A-2003-13864); Vino de Pago Calificado as the Village question c-uolx1t26 teaches. The Village chapters, INTRO_CLASS and the la-mancha trap already put Vino de Pago at the head, so the spain country record (the three named fields, its ladder and overview) and the two places that called DOCa the top tier of Spanish law now say the top regional tier.
applied.source: Ley 24/2003, de 10 de julio, de la Viña y del Vino, article 13 (boe.es, BOE-A-2003-13864); mapa.gob.es, Revista Española de Estudios Agrosociales y Pesqueros 204 (the levels of the 2003 law); searched 31 October 2026
